p: We have 3 currently on staff, yes. We have 2, uh, disability resource coordinators, we have a manager of that team, um, and then we've got, um, my understanding is 16 interns that are also serving as disability resource, uh, associates. They're interns, uh, who are all people with disability. Many of them are blind New Yorkers, and they're all based also— when they're working as part of their internship, we have them working at our Workforce One centers. And, and it's been an incredible partnership with the state's Commission, uh, for the Blind and Access-VR, where they're not only helping us be more thoughtful about being an employer that has New Yorkers working, uh, who are people with disability, but also on the flip side, how can we make sure for other blind New Yorkers and other New New Yorkers with disabilities when they experience that center. Are there things they're catching that we can then improve, uh, to make the experience better?
And for the internships, do you, uh, know if any of the interns have then gone on to, uh, retaining a job at the Workforce One Centers?
I'm not aware of that number. They're all currently interns, and it's a— it's state-funded internships, uh, as I understand that we've been able to work with.
Got it. So, SBS is not necessarily recruiting the interns.

No, we're recruiting the interns, but the funding sources from the state, because we don't— we really don't have, uh, city funding resources available for the operations of our centers. Most of our centers are completely, almost completely reliant on federal dollars, uh, and, and this partnership where we were able to expand the work of our 3-person team was the result of some state funding available at, uh, the State Commission for the Blind and, uh, at Access-VR. We do actually know that one, at least one of these interns was- will likely be hired at one of our Workforce One Centers.

That's great news. And so 3 staff members, do you think that that staffing level

is adequate and has that changed from the past? Is this an increase?

I think the number has, uh, hovered around 3 and 4. Um, we could always do more, uh, but, but with the resources that we've had, we've ensured and been very strategic with deploying them in ways in which to not just keep them in the central office at SBS, but leverage them to improve accessibility across the 17 centers. Office hours are a great way where we have 2 of these staff members doing multiple office hours at multiple centers instead of being fully located and deployed at one particular center.

Understood and then are there other kinds of internship opportunities that the— that you all are, uh, making accessible to folks with disabilities? Like, I think the SBS program is, is really wonderful to hear about. I did not know about that.

So I can speak for the— at Talent, um, we have the Partnership for Inclusive Internship that works, uh, with connecting people with disabilities to paid internships, primarily in the public sector. Um, like I mentioned earlier, we

fund the- the staff and the operational cost. It's through a great nonprofit partner, AHRC, who runs the program. Um, the funding for the wages are paid through the state VR agencies. And since March of, uh, 2024, over 109, uh, individuals with, uh, disabilities have been connected to internships and 54 of those, uh, 54 individuals have transitioned to permanent employment after completing their internships.
And you said that the— it's primarily public sector internships. Does that mean that folks went into working in city agencies, or—
So, it's primarily public sector internships, um, though 16 out of the 54 job placements have been with city agencies. The rest have been at other, uh, non-city agencies.
And, and do you know what the, uh, hourly wages are or were for those permanent placements?

The— for the permanent placements, it, it varies, uh, quite a bit because, um, there are, you know, er, like I mentioned, people with disabilities have a variety of different skill sets, experiences, and so, um, the jobs range, um,

from, you know, higher-wage IT, like cybersecurity jobs, to, uh, data management, to human resources, uh, to office and clerical work and project managers. So the wages range— the salary ranges from like the mid-$40,000 to upward of, uh, over, hmm, $100,000-plus, uh, dollars.
What happens to PII participants whose access VR eligibility is denied or whose access VR services are delayed? Does the city have a contingency funding mechanism to serve them?

So in order to be eligible for this particular program, uh, individuals do need to have that certification from the access VR agencies. Fortunately, AHRC is a great organization that, uh, operates our program, but also operates many other, uh, types of programming. So may be able to connect them to programming that they are serving or refer them to other types of programs that they may be eligible for.
What's the city's total, uh, annual contribution to PII, and what share of overall program funding does that city contribution represent?

So, uh, we contribute about $250,000 a year for the programming. Um, the wages— I don't have the exact numbers, um, but I think over uh, I'm not sure. I'll have to get back to you on what the, uh, exact costs on the wages are, though the wages are obviously a significant cost, um, because we wanna make sure that the— all of the interns are paid.
And, uh, is the city using, uh, PII to build a pop— a pipeline, excuse me, for its own agencies, or is it designed to place participants broadly?

We obviously wanna make sure that we are building the, uh, pipeline of city talent and, and creating an inclusive, uh, place to work for being the City of New York, being a model employer. And so we always wanna make sure that we are connecting city agencies to, uh, the job seekers. And so it is— the internships are primarily city agencies, not necessarily every job opportunity is, but that's also because of, you know, people choose to accept jobs or pursue jobs, um, in different sectors for, uh, a variety of, of reasons. And so some people wanna stay working for the city. Um, I

hope they do. I love working for the city, but people are also moving on to great opportunities outside of the city. I'll say one thing that even just hosting an intern, um, even if that intern, um, for one reason or another does not end up permanently working at that intern— it's a really great experience for that agency just from a cultural change, right? Of understanding um, sort of, you know, uh, getting rid of a lot of the- the misconceptions and assumptions that city agencies may have. So I would say even if those interns are not ultimately going to be hired or may not choose to work at that city agency, I think even just, uh, having an intern, um, who has a disability is a way that can really change behaviors of that city agency as to, like, we— that intern might have noticed that, oh, our documents we are creating are not necessarily accessible. And so let's just change the font size or the font type, right? And so things like that, I think, are, um, uh, a really good opportunity to, um, make sure that there's some cultural change happening within the city agencies so, um, we can continue to be an

inclusive, uh, employer. But I will say city agencies have also hired our PII interns. I know New York City Public Schools has hired, uh, a few interns and, um, uh, last month, 2 months ago when we had our co-design, uh, announcement, um, we had Committee staff there, which was an exciting announcement in partnership with all of the agencies here. Um, we had a representative from New York City Public Schools who went through the PII program and was connected to a job opportunity. And so we're, we're proud of that work and making sure that the city is, is being a model employer for all of the employers across the city.

Could you also just walk me through, for my own understanding, uh, how PII is operating, um, working with folks with disabilities? What, what is the role from start to end that PII is supporting in these internship placements?

So we fund the - through AHRC is the nonprofit that operates it and then they will— and it's— people can find out about it through a variety of sources, right? AHRC is a big nonprofit that already has some connections. We do a lot of work of advocating and

sharing that information to city agencies and through our, uh, QI Advisory Council, um, which is— includes employers, private sector employers as well, to make sure that they are aware of this program that it exists. And then an individual may be connected through a variety of ways, but there is even a, uh, an interest form on AHRC's website, and where if someone is interested can express and fill out that form and then potentially be connected to, uh, through PI. Or like I said, if, if for whatever reason, um, there's other services that might— that they might not be, uh, eligible, AHRC is a great organization that can help connect them to other programming as well. And then they will work at the intern— they're typically 4 to 6 month internships, and then AHRC works, uh, closely with them to try to help them, uh, secure, uh, employment as well.

Got it and so does PII, uh, what, or what kinds of, uh, materials are city agencies receiving or what's the information that you all are sharing with them? So we work with city agencies day in and day out, and so we'll always, uh, make sure to plug our, uh, PII program. I'll have to get back to you in terms of, like, specific

collateral, um, that may be available, though we do, um, touching on, um, something that came up earlier, the jobs.nyc.gov website is a useful tool for both employers and job seekers in terms of, uh, being able to, uh, connect to the suite of services offered across the city and all of the city agencies. So job seekers with disabilities and city agencies who are, uh, or rather employers who are looking for, uh, talent can go to that site and be connected through a variety of sources.

So the Civil Service Law 55A authorizes up to 200— uh, 700 designated positions as of November 2025, 363 employees were participating across 34 agencies. How many employees are currently participating in the 55A program across how many agencies?
Hi, I'm Katian Outar, I'm the Assistant Commissioner for the Workforce Operations team at DCAS. Um, currently we have, um, 368 individuals participating across 36 agencies as of the end of March.
Got it and what's preventing, uh, the program from reaching its 700-position, uh, statutory ceiling?

I think one of the challenges that the program really fluctuates over time. So as we add new folks to the program, there are folks that are leaving the program. So for example, we may have, uh, new hires that are coming in. We have approximately 30 that were hired last year, but we have about 50 folks that are being— that are removed from the program, either because of promotion, because they have been— they left the agency, they retired, or they are serving in a different title. So it really fluctuates. Um, so we know that, uh, additional engagement is needed to, you know, really get to that number but we have to kind of like double the goals if we want to get to the 700.
And are you all keeping track of who's getting promoted or how many folks have left the city job? Like, are you keeping track of those, uh, various criteria?

Yes, so we work with the agencies. When somebody leaves the program, we get a, um, the reason as to whether it was because of a retirement, because they went into a different position, or they took a civil service exam and received a promotion in that way. So we do track that.
So you track that. Are you able to share that with us?

Um, I can share with you. So for example, last, um, across the last 2 years, we had about 98 people that left the program for various reasons, but we can give you a, um, a greater breakdown, um, after this.
That'd be great. And then how are you all, um, uh, recruiting qualified candidates?

So one of the things that work really well is the partnerships that we have with MOPD, um, and also with our partner agencies. Um, the way the program is set up— and just to clarify, this is a program that allows individuals to be hired into city government positions and competitive positions without the need to take a civil service exam. So the hiring still happens at the agency level. Individuals— agencies still have to have, you know, OMB approval, they have to have a line, um, and individuals still have to go through the interview process and get selected. And then the agencies will, uh, submit their application for us to process.

So what we do to supplement just awareness of the program is through a partnership with MOPD, we'll do, um, information sessions. We do that closely with their staff that are, are, um, involved in the program. So their job seekers that are involved in the program. We also do, um, just our general outreach to, uh, populations that are— whether it's educational institutions, community-based organizations to make sure that a lot of folks are aware. So we'll have those targeted information sessions, targeted outreach, but, um, the program sits within the Office of Citywide Recruitment, and we do about, um, 15 to 20 events per month, and that's embedded in the information that we share with job seekers.
Wait, what does the Office of Citywide Recruitment do?

So our main job is to go out into the, um, public and really speak about the jobs that are available within city government. So we promote the civil service exams, the process for taking those exams, the different types

of positions available across agencies, and kind of like what that application process is.
And is that also happening in collaboration with the Workforce One centers?

Yes, we have a very robust relationship with the Workforce Ones where we either go to the sites depending on um, the interest that we have. So we'll go either in person or we'll have virtual sessions. Um, and for the last 2 years, we've been robustly working on a schedule to make sure we're engaging folks there.

I want to recognize we've been joined by Council Member Rita Joseph. Um, and how many city staff are dedicated to, uh, promoting the 55A program at DCAS and MOPD, uh, respectively? And does the Admin believe current staffing sufficient to drive a— to drive broader agency participation?

So, currently, we have, uh, staff that is managing the application process from beginning to end, but because the program is embedded into the Office of Citywide Recruitment, which has about, um, 5 staff in terms of promotion, um, that's spread across. So, every time, um, a recr— uh, we

have what we call citywide inclusive recruiters. Every time they go out into the public, they're sharing information about the program.
The citywide inclusive recruiters, how many?
So we have 3 citywide inclusive, um, recruitment specialists. Um, we have a civil service pathway fellow as well as a deputy director, um, within the Office of Citywide Recruitment.
And the citywide inclusive specialists, uh, could you share a little bit more about what they do in the field?

Yeah, so their main role is to make sure that the public is aware of city jobs. Um, we know a lot of the challenges that we have with hiring just across the board is that folks are not familiar with the civil service exams. And when they think about city government, they may only think about, uh, specific titles. So we do civil service 101 information sessions where we're really just breaking down, uh, the beginning. Here's what city government looks like. Here are the jobs that you can get into. Here's what the civil service exam looks like. Here's when the

schedule is come— is out. Here's fee waivers. Here's more information about the 55A program. So we really give an overall, um, view of what it means to work for the city. We also partner with our community partners, educational institutions. Um, we attend career fairs, we do panel conversations, we do a lot of different activities to make sure that folks are aware of city government and the jobs that they can do there.
And so that's mostly, uh, through invitations, or do they also have just like outreach hours where they're in a neighborhood, in a community?

We do it all across the 5 boroughs and virtually. So for example, um, we have specific demographics that we're trying to reach, including people with disabilities, veterans, um, those that are underrepresented in city government. So we do outreach to make sure that we are targeting those populations. So we'd work with, um, let's say DOE, or we work with a shelter to make sure that we're engaging their populations. And then we also get invitations to participate in different events.
I will now pass it to Council Member Joseph to ask her questions if she's ready.

Oh yeah, I'm ready. Good morning. Um, morning? Yes, afternoon. I have a couple of questions around transportation. Um, I noticed mostly around elevator outages on MTA subways remain a documented barrier to employment for New Yorkers with mobility disability. Does the city have a formal coordination? Do you work in partnership with, um, MTA to maybe do an assessment to see where they are in key locations as to where we can create barriers? For example, in my district, I only had one elevator that was accessible. For 2 years we worked with MTA, we finally got a second one. Are you looking around the city at the ecosystem of transportation? That's one of the biggest barriers, including for New York City students. And we've heard that, um, across the city— CUNY students, um, New York City Public School students who cannot sometimes have no routes to get to their destination. So how are we working with agent— interagency to make sure that accessibility for transportation across the

board are available for New Yorkers with disabilities?

So I will, um, uh, er, I'm the Commissioner of, um, ah, Disabilities, and we have a regular meeting with, ah, um, MTA, ah, people involved, and this is the first, um, ah, thing that we, um, mentioned, because even for me, um,— when I worked at the Health Department, there was no— there was one elevator, and then there was another elevator that'd be better, that was closer, and then they finally did it, and it was like a revelation. I could ha— I could go in one direction, I can go in another direction, it was great. So we're working with them on that, and we're hoping to resolve it. To be fair, MTA, um, does, uh, prioritize this work, um, and so we're hoping they will continue to prioritize this, especially in, um, uh, areas that is, uh, really needed. So I'm- I'm gonna keep pushing.

Uh, oh yeah, we'll keep pushing as well. Um, but is there a dollar amount attached to this work? For example, I had set a goal with New York City Public School when I was the Education Chair to make sure that buildings are

accessible by 2030 for all New York City students with a billion-dollar investment. What does that look like on your end?
Um, I don't know, but I will find out, um, from MTA and for our, our, um, work as well.

Thank you. I had a question about, um, cliff benefit— benefit cliffs. Um, the risk of losing SSDI, SSI, Medicaid eligibility upon entering the workforce is one of the most frequently cited barriers to employment for people with disabilities. Which city programs specifically address the benefit cliff and how?

Hi, I'm, I'm Abby Mayerhoff, the Director of Programs for NYC at Work. Um, so I can speak on behalf of, of our program and the resources that we utilize. Um, within our staff, we have, uh, someone who is a benefits counselor, and so she provides individual advisement to, um, participants of our program. Um, and we also work closely with the Department of Consumer and Worker Protection. Um, about 7 years ago, uh, MOPD and DCWP partnered to, uh, pilot a financial counseling program that was tailored specifically for individuals with disabilities.
Mhm.

Um, and the result of that pilot, uh, led to a training that has been implemented for all of the financial counselors. Um, and DCWP can certainly explain more about that, but we work in partnership with those counselors and with DCWP to ensure that individuals who participate in our program have access to that financial counseling as well. It's not as in-depth as benefits counseling, but it's a really great, um, first step for most individuals who we interact with on that.
And how do you do your outreach and engagement with communities with disabilities?

In general for the NYC at Work program? Uh, we say yes to almost every invitation we receive. Uh, we go to a lot of community events, so that's hosted by CBOs, schools, colleges. Um, just last week we were at, um, uh, CUNY Leads, uh, career fair.
I was there.

Oh, we were there. Uh, sorry, we didn't have a chance to meet then. Um, we host information sessions for a lot of our community

partners, um, and then we respond to individual outreach as well.
And, and, and, and, uh, community members with disabilities and English is not their first language, how do you reach them?

Sorry, one moment. Um, so we utilize language access, and, um, the reality is that even ASL, um, are not like— there's different languages in ASL. And so that's like an interesting, um, next step for us to think about how can language access and ASL, for example, um, uh, expand that, um, reach about, uh, language access and ASL and other forms of language.

Very important for our communities. Um, the SNAP work requirement goes into effect in March of 2026. New Yorkers with disability can, uh, request exemptions, um, but most document— but must document them. What is the Administration, um, doing to ensure that participants in disability employment program who receive SNAP understand the exemption right and do not lose food assistance? Are city programs being used to help our community with disabilities? That's very important.

Yeah, it's very important. Um, so, uh, uh, we are working— meaning all the agencies are working, um, and, uh, DSS is the lead on this. And every agency or office like ours have, um, uh, have to think about our population, in our case disability communities, it's complicated because a lot of them will be exempt, but some may not. And so, um, we're, uh, discussing that with the DSS people on, um, how can we, um, uh, use that, uh, those few people that may get— not get exempt, and could we make it zero. Like, that would be fantastic, but like, we want to discuss that with them in more detail.
Are you also working with ACS for young people who are in foster care who have disability?
Yeah, and, um, uh, we're also— the DYCD, um, also is very engaged on this topic as well, and I'm, um, going to meet with her soon.
So ACS, DSS, all of the agencies should be working together.
Yeah.

And how are we recruiting, um, people with disabilities and training

to, to enter the workforce and, and live independent lives? And I know that, um, some of the programs also live in the New York City public schools and creating them, making them independent, learning to travel and all of that other stuff, and life skills are being taught. How is that partnership working to enter work for the workforce?
Um, meaning, uh, for high school people?
High school students, internships, apprenticeships. Sometimes our communities with disabilities don't get these opportunities for internships, apprenticeships, how does that work?

Yeah, so, um, I think we can share some examples of internships and stuff that we've had, but personally it matters a lot. The transition from high school to, um, further school or, um, employment is like, uh, can be enhanced because, um, that is what is happening is like this cliff that people graduate from col— uh, high school and then where they go. And so that is one of the areas that, um, MOPD wants to get more involved on

that with, um, the schools and, uh, er, ah, specifically the, um, special ed people.

Yeah, definitely. Um, there's always a gap there. There's a, there's a huge gap there with our students with disabilities who I hear all the time from who the pathway into college, the pathway into career is not readily available to them because of disabilities. So I think that's where the gap is. And I think, um, talking into— with other agencies and figuring out a comprehensive plan, not a piecemeal, but a comprehensive plan across the board for, um, our communities who are living with disabilities. Thank you so much. Thank you, Chair.

Thank you. Okay, uh, my final few questions, uh, going back to the 55A program: which agencies are the largest participants in the 55A program, and which, uh, large city agencies have little to no 55A representation?

Thank you. Um, I see the 55A program and the usage of it is spread across, um, uh, most of our agencies. We'll see the larger agencies do have the higher numbers because of just the vacancies and the amount of positions that they are—

they're hiring. Um, but what we also know is that although individuals may not be serving in the 55A program, they're still being hired, um, because they could be hired into a noncompetitive title or, um, an exempt or a labor title.
But given you all are keeping, uh, a record of the, uh, positions that are coming through the 55A program, are you, are you not keeping track of where they're spread across in the city agencies?
Yes. So for the individuals that are serving in, um, the top agencies, and these are individuals that have more than 25, um, participants, as I mentioned, there'll be—
Which agencies?
Our social services agencies like, um, Department of Social Services, we have NYPD, Department of Education, um, DOHMH, Department of Finance. So the larger agencies—
I think I'm just trying to understand exactly which agencies are bringing, uh, or hiring, um, through the 55A program and which are not?

Yes. So the- the agencies that I just listed are the- the top agencies that have the higher numbers. Um, and then there are also some of the larger agencies as well. And so as it relates to, um, how there are, um, individuals that are using it robustly and individuals that we're working with to enhance their use of the program.
And which agencies would you say that- that includes in terms of the enhancement?

Um, so in terms of the enhancements in different agencies that we've worked with, um, we try to spread it across the board. Um, say for example, uh, DCAS, one of the things that we do within DCAS is we have, um, agency-specific hiring events. And so we've seen that across the years, like where we may have, um, been at maybe 6 or 7, um, 2, 3 years ago. Now we're at 15, 16. So we're seeing those engagements and partnerships with, um, MOPD to really increase the partnership across the agencies and their usage of the program.

Yeah, I'd re— I'd really be interested in knowing, um, the specificity here, uh, just to see how we're doing as a, as a city in terms

of hiring and, uh, retention, um, and understanding exactly why some agencies have been more, uh, proactive, or are the specific roles related to, um, the kind of, uh, positions that folks with disabilities have been able to apply for. So I think that that is a- is a very important, um, data set. Um, the July 2025 55A Diversity Career Fair produced 13 conditional job offers from 15 participating agencies, with 5 agencies conducting on-the-spot interviews. Why did 10 of the 15 agencies participate without conducting interviews, and what follow-up occurred with those agencies after the fair?

Um, so when we have our citywide— and, um, MOPD can add into that— but when we have our citywide events, um, not all agencies may readily have OMB approval for their vacancies, and so agencies, and depending on the amount of positions that they are recruiting for, um, they may choose to conduct on-spot— on-the-site, um, interviews or hire. For the ones that do not, um, we do follow up with them to see, like, what's the engagement after.
What's the OMB relationship again?
So, um, positions still have to be OMB approved, um, so there's still that financial, um, approval that's needed for anyone— that's hired into the 55A program.
So you're saying that agencies that haven't gotten approval are conducting interview— are not conducting interviews?
They may not do interviews on the spot, but they're still doing interviews in through their normal course of business.
Got it, got it. So specifically an OMB-related issue?

Um, sometimes that is the reason. It's not the only reason. Some agencies, again, depending on the dynamic and the positions that they're looking for in their interview process. They may decide to do their interviews internally, but they do participate to share information about their particular jobs. They may have different positions that are available. Um, one of the things that we also do is we try to do exact matching. So the candidates that are showing up may have, um, direct match to a position. Some agencies may not have a lot of matches to their

positions, but they're still able to engage with different, um, with different job seekers based on other opportunities that they have. And I'll pass it over to Abby.

Thank you. Um, I'll also add that in the course of our follow-up with job seekers and participating agencies, there were multiple agencies that did conduct additional interviews following the recruitment event itself, and the agencies ultimately just decided to go with other, um, candidates. Um, but, you know, as I think we mentioned before, the process of going through those interviews and, and moving ahead in the hiring process is - is, you know, valuable for, for those individuals as well.
Absolutely. And so, uh, for this specific, uh, career fair, do you know what follow-up occurred with the agencies, uh, afterward?

So I can speak for NYC at Work. Um, we follow up with the agencies afterwards to get a sense in terms of, generally speaking, whether or not candidates that they met with were prepared for the event, were they a match for the positions that they have available, um, how, you know, whether they

were interested in them for either their existing positions or other positions, um, and then individual follow-up to try to get some feedback on specific candidates who may be moving forward in the hiring process, um, to help, um, with that as well. And then I'll turn to DCAS for anything additional.

Yes, and for the candidates that are hired, we kind of work with them throughout the 55A application process to make sure that they are able to be onboarded, you know, once there's, um, approval for the- for the positions. Um, so we wanna make sure that that process is seamless for them.
Understood and, uh, could you just clarify MOPD's relationship again with the 55A program?

Sure. Uh, so we work in partnership with DCAS to promote the program, both with city agencies and to job seekers. Um, support with the, um, application and onboarding, um, and then navigating some of the additional hurdles that may come with getting hired at the city.

Well, that's all I've got for today. Thank you all so much. We'll take a very quick 2-minute break.

You may also email written testimony to testimony@council.nyc.gov within 72 hours of this hearing. Audio and video recordings will not be accepted. I wanna bring up the first in-person panel. Evan

Yankee, Anthony Phillips, Kathleen Collins, Belkys Garcia. Absolutely, absolutely. Yeah, no worries. Gregory Meves. Whenever you're ready.

Good morning, uh, my name is Evan Yankey, and I am the Advocacy Director at the Brooklyn Center for Independence of the Disabled, an independent living center supporting people with disabilities in Brooklyn and beyond. People with disabilities face tremendous barriers to equal economic opportunity, including foremost discrimination, which is typically cited as most impactful in surveys, and transportation accessibility. Today, though, I want to talk about one particular barrier. As you may be aware, 19 disability and labor groups have joined us to write and advocate in opposition to Intro 303, a bill penalizing people with disabilities for receiving 24-hour live-in home care. This bill, if passed, will penalize people with disabilities and care providers for providing care that is assigned to them by managed long-term care plans. People with disabilities in consumer-directed care will be fined $500 a day. Home care workers

will lose jobs as home care agencies pull out of work rather than face fines. The supporters of this bill claim that home care agencies will be able to easily switch 24-hour live-in shifts to 12-hour split shifts, but this is not true. It is unbelievable to anyone who has advocated for a fairer, more progressive Medicaid system, and it should be unbelievable to City Council members. We suspect many elected officials know better but are wary of crossing mobilized groups who don't. I'm holding up a Medicaid authorization. This is the form that assigns a person with a disability 24-hour live-in care through no choice of their own. The authorization is typically given by a managed long-term care plan and determines the type of care that you get. You cannot change it on your own. Home care agencies cannot change it. But the benefit amount at $170 a week is so low that it would make more financial sense for her to accept the part-time work schedule her employer offered than to apply for TDI, even at risk of further compromising her health.
